9701-3.4.1.motivate: Almost every molecule you will meet for the rest of this course is held together by shared pairs of electrons. Get the definition and the electron counting right here and dot-and-cross diagrams, shapes and bond energies all follow.
9701-3.4.1.establish:
**Covalent bonding** is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and a shared pair of electrons. It is a force: name both the nuclei and the shared pair.

One shared pair is a single bond: $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{Cl2}$, $\ce{HCl}$, $\ce{CH4}$, $\ce{C2H6}$. Two are a double bond: $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{C2H4}$, and two double bonds in $\ce{CO2}$. Three are a triple bond, as in $\ce{N2}$. $\ce{NH3}$ has three bonding pairs plus a lone pair on nitrogen, and each shared pair counts two electrons for both bonded atoms.

Period 3 elements can **expand the octet**: sulfur has 10 outer electrons in $\ce{SO2}$ and 12 in $\ce{SF6}$, phosphorus 10 in $\ce{PCl5}$. A period 2 atom cannot exceed eight.

In a **coordinate (dative covalent) bond** both electrons of the shared pair come from one atom: a lone pair is donated into an empty orbital on the acceptor. $\ce{NH3}$ and $\ce{HCl}$ gases react because the nitrogen lone pair is donated to $\ce{H+}$, giving $\ce{NH4+}$ with one coordinate bond — all four $\ce{N-H}$ bonds are then identical. In $\ce{Al2Cl6}$ each $\ce{AlCl3}$ unit donates a chlorine lone pair to the aluminium of the other: two coordinate bonds.
9701-3.4.1.connect: Electronegativity difference decided whether bonding is ionic or covalent (3.1); counting bonding pairs and lone pairs here is exactly what 3.5 uses to predict shapes and 3.7 uses to draw dot-and-cross diagrams.
9701-3.4.1.note:
- Covalent bond: electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and a shared pair of electrons.
- Single $=$ 1 shared pair, double $=$ 2, triple $=$ 3; a shared pair counts for both atoms.
- Period 3 can expand the octet: $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{PCl5}$ 10 electrons, $\ce{SF6}$ 12.
- Coordinate bond: both electrons from one atom, a lone pair into an empty orbital.
- $\ce{NH3 + H+ -> NH4+}$ has one coordinate bond; $\ce{Al2Cl6}$ has two.
9701-3.4.1.self_explain: Why does $\ce{NH4+}$ behave as though it has four identical bonds, even though one of them was formed as a coordinate bond?

discover.stem: Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas form solid ammonium chloride. How many coordinate (dative covalent) bonds are in one $\ce{NH4+}$ ion?

options.A: 0, because every bond needs one electron from each atom
options.D: 4, because all four bonds are identical

discover.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair is donated to $\ce{H+}$, which brings no electrons, so exactly one of the four bonds is formed as a coordinate bond. Once formed, all four $\ce{N-H}$ bonds are identical, but only one was made by donation.

9701-3.4.2.motivate: Papers ask you to count $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds in an unfamiliar molecule almost every session. The counting takes seconds once you know that each pair of bonded atoms shares exactly one $\sigma$ bond.
9701-3.4.2.establish:
Bonds form by **orbital overlap**. A **$\sigma$ bond** is formed by direct overlap of orbitals between the bonding atoms, along the line joining the nuclei. A **$\pi$ bond** is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals, giving electron density above and below the $\sigma$ bond.

So every bond between two atoms, including every $\ce{C-H}$ bond, contains one $\sigma$ bond: single $=1\sigma$, double $=1\sigma+1\pi$, triple $=1\sigma+2\pi$. $\ce{H2}$: one $\sigma$ bond from 1s overlap. $\ce{C2H6}$: 7 $\sigma$ bonds. $\ce{C2H4}$: 5 $\sigma$ and 1 $\pi$. $\ce{HCN}$: 2 $\sigma$ and 2 $\pi$. $\ce{N2}$: 1 $\sigma$ and 2 $\pi$.

**Hybridisation** mixes one s orbital with p orbitals to give equivalent orbitals that make the $\sigma$ bonds. An atom forming four $\sigma$ bonds is $sp^3$ (tetrahedral, as in $\ce{C2H6}$); three $\sigma$ bonds gives $sp^2$ (three orbitals in a plane at $120°$, as in $\ce{C2H4}$); two $\sigma$ bonds gives sp (linear, as in $\ce{HCN}$). The p orbitals left unhybridised are the ones that overlap sideways to make the $\pi$ bonds, which is why ethene is planar and ethane is not.
9701-3.4.2.connect: The $\sigma$ framework fixes the shapes of 3.5, and the $\pi$ bond of $\ce{C=C}$ is the reactive site of every alkene reaction in organic chemistry.
9701-3.4.2.note:
- $\sigma$ bond: direct, end-on overlap of orbitals between the bonding atoms.
- $\pi$ bond: sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals, above and below the $\sigma$ bond.
- Single $1\sigma$; double $1\sigma+1\pi$; triple $1\sigma+2\pi$; $\ce{C-H}$ bonds are $\sigma$ bonds.
- $\ce{C2H4}$: 5 $\sigma$, 1 $\pi$. $\ce{HCN}$: 2 $\sigma$, 2 $\pi$. $\ce{N2}$: 1 $\sigma$, 2 $\pi$.
- $\sigma$ bonds at an atom: 4 is $sp^3$, 3 is $sp^2$, 2 is sp.
9701-3.4.2.self_explain: Why can a $\pi$ bond never exist on its own between two atoms that are not already joined by a $\sigma$ bond?

discover.stem: How many $\sigma$ bonds and how many $\pi$ bonds are in one molecule of ethene, $\ce{C2H4}$?
discover.explanation: Four $\ce{C-H}$ bonds plus the $\sigma$ part of the $\ce{C=C}$ bond give 5 $\sigma$ bonds, and the second shared pair of the double bond is the single $\pi$ bond.

9701-3.4.3.motivate: Nitrogen makes up most of the air yet does almost nothing, while oxygen rusts iron and burns fuels. The difference is one number: the energy needed to break the bond.
9701-3.4.3.establish:
**Bond energy** is the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state. It is an energy *input*, so it is endothermic and quoted as a positive value, such as $E(\ce{Cl-Cl})=+244$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. **Bond length** is the internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms.

The two are linked. The more shared pairs between the same two nuclei, the shorter the bond and the larger the bond energy: $\ce{C-C}$ 154 pm and 350 kJ mol$^{-1}$, $\ce{C=C}$ 134 pm and 610, $\ce{C#C}$ 120 pm and 840. Longer bonds between larger atoms are weaker: $\ce{Cl-Cl}$ 244, $\ce{Br-Br}$ 193, $\ce{I-I}$ 151 kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Use this to compare reactivity. A reaction usually starts by breaking a bond, so a large bond energy means a molecule that reacts only under extreme conditions: $\ce{N#N}$ at 994 kJ mol$^{-1}$ leaves nitrogen inert at room temperature, while $\ce{O=O}$ at 496 reacts readily, and $\ce{I2}$ dissociates most easily of the halogens. For a stated amount, multiply moles of bonds by the bond energy: 2.0 mol of $\ce{NH3}$ holds 6.0 mol of $\ce{N-H}$ bonds, so $6.0\times391=2346$ kJ.
9701-3.4.3.connect: These bond energies are the numbers you will put into enthalpy-change calculations in 4.1, and bond polarity in 3.6 explains why two bonds of similar energy can still react very differently.
9701-3.4.3.note:
- Bond energy: energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state.
- Bond length: the internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms.
- More shared pairs means shorter bond means higher bond energy.
- Stronger bond means harder to break means less reactive: $\ce{N2}$ 994 against $\ce{O2}$ 496 kJ mol$^{-1}$.
- Energy to break $n$ mol of a substance $=n\times$(bonds per molecule)$\times$ bond energy, in kJ.
9701-3.4.3.self_explain: Why must bond energy be defined for the gaseous state rather than for a liquid or a solid?

discover.stem: The $\ce{Cl-Cl}$, $\ce{Br-Br}$ and $\ce{I-I}$ bond energies are 244, 193 and 151 kJ mol$^{-1}$. Which molecule splits into atoms most readily, and why?

options.A: $\ce{Cl2}$, because its bond is the longest
options.B: $\ce{Cl2}$, because its bond energy is the largest
options.C: $\ce{I2}$, because its bond is the longest and weakest
options.D: They split equally readily, because each has one single bond

discover.explanation: Atoms get larger down the group, so the internuclear distance rises and the attraction holding the atoms together weakens; the $\ce{I-I}$ bond has the lowest bond energy and so breaks most readily.
